title: Futures rebound sharply after Wall Street's worst week since 2020
dek: US stock futures are up between 2% and 3% before Monday's open, led by Nasdaq and chip stocks, after last week's AI-driven selloff pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into a correction. Bonds and gold are reversing some of last week's moves, and traders now see a December Fed hike as nearly certain.
quick: Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 3.3% and S&P 500 futures about 2.5%, per Reuters, after the S&P fell seven days in a row.
Nvidia is up roughly 8% to 9% pre-market after President Trump urged its board to rehire Jensen Huang; the board says it will not.
CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion; Zscaler is up double digits, CrowdStrike down.
Treasury yields are higher as safety demand fades: the 2-year is near 4.69% and the 10-year near 4.96%. Fed funds futures put a December hike at about 96%.
Gold is up about 2% near $3,600 and Bitcoin is back above $61,000 after hitting a two-year low Saturday. Oil is little changed.
Today: flash PMIs at 9:45 a.m. ET, New York Fed President Williams at 4 p.m., and Agilent and Zoom after the close. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving.

blocks.head: A relief rally follows the worst week for US stocks in more than five years
blocks.what: Index futures climbed overnight after Friday's selloff left the S&P 500 at 6,910.39 and the Dow at 48,147.33, both more than 10% below their records. Reuters reported Nasdaq 100 futures up 3.3% and S&P 500 futures up 2.5% as of early European trading, with Dow futures up about 2%. The Nasdaq Composite lost about 10% last week, its biggest weekly drop since March 2020, and the VIX volatility index briefly topped 40 for the first time since April 2025, per Reuters.
blocks.why: A rebound of this size would recover a large part of Friday's losses, with chipmakers and other AI-linked stocks expected to lead because they fell the most. Safe-haven assets like Treasurys and the yen are giving back some of last week's gains as money moves back toward stocks.
blocks.watch: Strategists are split. Goldman Sachs' trading desk called the selloff a buying opportunity, while other analysts cited by Reuters cautioned that sharp bounces during a correction can fade. Whether the gains hold through Wednesday's inflation data is the main test.

blocks.head: Nvidia jumps as Washington's tone on Jensen Huang shifts
blocks.what: Nvidia shares rose roughly 8% to 9% in pre-market trading after President Trump posted that the board should bring back Jensen Huang as CEO, saying it would be best for the company and the country. Nvidia's board chair has said the board accepted Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him, and the company has hired search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CBS that Huang is now outside the company and that it is too soon to say whether he should return, while calling on Nvidia to answer questions about chip sales to China. Reports of an SEC inquiry into the company's disclosures and accounting, first reported by the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, have not been confirmed by the company or the agency.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, so its swings move the whole market and the chip sector with it. The stock had fallen about 19% in three sessions before today, according to market data cited by several outlets, making it the center of last week's AI selloff.
blocks.watch: Any statement from the board, Huang or regulators. Prediction-market odds of Huang returning rose to about 16% from under 10% last week, per one report.

blocks.head: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock
blocks.what: CrowdStrike announced an all-stock deal to acquire Zscaler, confirming talks first reported Friday by Bloomberg and Reuters. Zscaler holders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share, which values Zscaler at about $260.41 a share, a 34% premium to its last close, per Reuters. Zscaler shares rose roughly 13% to 16% pre-market, depending on the source, while CrowdStrike fell about 5% to 9%.
blocks.why: This is one of the largest cybersecurity deals on record and combines endpoint protection with network security. It could lift other security software stocks on takeover speculation. CrowdStrike's drop reflects the dilution from issuing new shares and investor doubts about the price.
blocks.watch: Regulatory review and whether CrowdStrike's falling share price narrows the premium Zscaler holders actually receive, since the deal is paid in stock.

blocks.head: Fed hike odds climb as bond buyers step back
blocks.what: Treasury yields rose as investors moved out of safe havens. CNBC reported the 2-year yield up about 7 basis points to 4.689% and the 10-year up about 4 basis points to 4.959%. Fed funds futures now price about a 96% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the December 8-9 meeting, up from about 92% Friday, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
blocks.why: Higher expected rates raise borrowing costs and weigh on stock valuations, especially for high-growth tech. A near-certain December hike means Wednesday's PCE inflation data mostly shapes expectations for January and beyond.
blocks.watch: New York Fed President John Williams speaks at 4 p.m. ET. He said on November 17 that conditions do not call for dramatic action, while Governor Christopher Waller has raised the idea of a half-point move.

blocks.head: Gulf attacks keep oil supported despite supply glut
blocks.what: The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported several attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Saudi Arabia said it destroyed a drone launched by Iran-backed Houthis, and Bahrain said an industrial facility was hit by Iranian projectiles, per CNBC. Iran said it remains open to a deal with the US.
blocks.why: The attacks add a risk premium to oil, but forecasts of a global surplus, including an IEA estimate of about 2 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter, have kept prices in a range. Energy stocks and inflation expectations both depend on which force wins out.
blocks.watch: Any disruption to tanker traffic through Hormuz, and whether US-Iran talks resume.

blocks.text: Asia

Asia was split. Japan's markets were closed for a public holiday, so the Nikkei 225 stays at Friday's level of about 56,437 after its 5.1% drop. South Korea's KOSPI fell another 3.3% to about 4,709 after dropping more than 5% during the session, extending losses in memory-chip stocks such as SK Hynix. Taiwan's Taiex rebounded about 2.2% to 36,812 after regulators banned short selling below the previous close and raised margin requirements, and the government said its stabilization fund was already buying. Hong Kong and mainland China moved less than 1% in either direction, with reports differing on the exact closing levels.
Europe

European stocks are up modestly, lagging the US futures bounce. The Stoxx 600 was about 0.5% higher in morning trade after its steepest weekly fall since March 2025, a drop of 5.8%. Germany's DAX was up about 0.3% to 0.5% and the FTSE 100 slightly higher, while Italy's FTSE MIB was the weakest major market, down about 0.9%. Early flash PMI surveys showed eurozone business activity holding up in November, though reports said the strength came mostly from Germany while France remained in contraction.
Currencies

The dollar is steady to slightly weaker overall, with the dollar index near 103.7, and CNBC described its recent rally as pausing. The yen, last week's main safe haven, is weakening again as investors return to risk: the dollar is near 159 yen, up from about 158.6 on Friday and close to the 160 level traders watch for possible Japanese intervention. The euro is near $1.10, the pound around $1.31, and the dollar is little changed against China's yuan near 6.67.

US stock futures are sharply higher ahead of the 9:30 a.m. ET open. The Nasdaq 100 is leading, up more than 3% according to Reuters and other outlets, because the stocks hit hardest last week, chips and AI names, are bouncing the most. The S&P 500 is up about 2.5% and the Dow roughly 2%. If those gains hold, the S&P 500 would open around 7,100, still well below its record.

The bounce is broad but uneven. Small caps are rising less than large tech, and the VIX should ease from Friday's close near 36 if the rally holds. Thin holiday trading can magnify moves in both directions this week, so early gains can shift quickly.

Treasurys are selling off after a five-day rally, pushing yields higher. The 2-year yield, which tracks Fed expectations most closely, rose about 7 basis points to near 4.69%, per CNBC. The 10-year rose about 4 basis points to near 4.96%, and the 30-year is little changed near 5.34%. Because short-term yields are rising faster than long-term ones, the curve is flattening slightly: the 10-year now pays roughly 27 basis points more than the 2-year.

Markets see the Fed raising rates again in December. Fed funds futures price about a 96% chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting, up from about 92% Friday, according to CME FedWatch data cited by CNBC. Officials disagree on the pace. Governor Christopher Waller has argued a half-point move may be needed, while New York Fed President John Williams said last week that conditions do not call for dramatic action. Last week's stock selloff has not changed those expectations much because inflation and growth data have stayed firm.
Fed speakers

items: Today, 4 p.m. ET: New York Fed President John Williams, a permanent voting member on rates.
Wednesday, 2 p.m. ET: Beige Book survey of regional business conditions.
Saturday, November 28: Fed officials enter the quiet period before the December meeting.

blocks.text: Sectors (Friday's session)

Technology was the weakest S&P 500 sector Friday, down about 7.3% as chipmakers sold off. Industrials (down 3.1%), consumer discretionary (down 3.0%), communication services (down 2.7%) and materials (down 2.2%) also lagged, all groups tied to AI spending or big tech. Consumer staples was the only sector to rise, up about 0.7%, while health care was nearly flat and energy, utilities and real estate fell less than 1%. This morning's futures suggest that pattern could reverse at least partly, with tech and chips leading and defensive sectors lagging.
Pre-market movers

items: Nvidia: up about 8% to 9% after President Trump called for Jensen Huang's return; the board has said it will not reinstate him.
Zscaler: up roughly 13% to 16% on the $43.9 billion all-stock takeover by CrowdStrike.
CrowdStrike: down about 5% to 9% after announcing the Zscaler deal.
Anthropic: up about 4%, per CNBC, after a rough first week of trading following its IPO.
Truist and Citizens Financial: each up more than 2% after Baird upgraded the regional banks to outperform.
LuxExperience: up about 6.6% after JPMorgan upgraded the online luxury retailer to overweight.
Chip stocks broadly: Micron, AMD and other semiconductor names are expected to rebound after losses of 13% to 14% Friday.

blocks.text: Oil

Crude is little changed, with Brent near $92 a barrel and WTI near $83. Both benchmarks fell about 4% to 5% last week, their third straight weekly decline. Weekend attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz and on Gulf facilities are supporting prices, while forecasts of a global supply surplus are holding them back. Analysts cited by several outlets expect a range-bound market through year-end.
Gold

Gold is up about 2% to around $3,600 an ounce after hitting a 14-month low near $3,503 last week. The bounce comes as the dollar rally pauses, per CNBC. Gold has struggled this month because expectations of more Fed hikes make a metal that pays no interest less attractive, and some investors sold it to cover losses elsewhere. It remains well below the $4,000 level it fell under on November 11.
Crypto

Bitcoin is trading around $61,300, more than 11% above the two-year low of about $55,100 it hit early Saturday, according to CoinDesk. Ether is up about 5% near $1,730. Analysts note sentiment is still weak: spot bitcoin ETFs have seen nearly $3 billion in outflows this month, per one report, and crypto has tracked tech stocks closely during the selloff.
A light day for data, with the Fed and earnings the bigger draws:

items: 9:45 a.m. ET: S&P Global flash PMIs for November. Forecasts call for manufacturing at 54.5, down from 56.0, and services at 55.6, down from 57.9. Readings above 50 mean expansion; a sharper slowdown would ease pressure on the Fed.
4 p.m. ET: New York Fed President John Williams speaks. Listen for whether he backs a quarter-point December hike or leaves room for more.
After the close: Agilent and Zoom report earnings.

blocks.text: Today's schedule is light. The two most closely watched reports both come after the close; dates are confirmed by company announcements and earnings calendars.

rows: Lab-equipment demand from drug and research customers; analysts expect about $1.72 to $1.73 a share on revenue near $1.98 billion to $1.99 billion.
Enterprise customer growth, its Anthropic investment and its outlook; analysts expect about $1.49 a share on $1.28 billion in revenue, after recent estimate cuts.

blocks.text: It is a holiday-shortened week: US stock markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday. Tuesday brings Analog Devices before the open and Dell and Workday after the close, the first big tests of AI hardware and business software demand since the selloff, plus Conference Board consumer confidence, forecast at 92.1. Wednesday is the key day: the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, forecast at 3.5% annualized, October PCE inflation, with core prices expected up 0.3% for the month, plus jobless claims and durable goods orders, all at 8:30 a.m. ET, followed by the Beige Book. Deere and Best Buy also report this week, and Black Friday sales on Friday will offer an early read on holiday spending.

bottom_line: The tone this morning is a rebound, not a reversal: futures are recovering part of last week's losses, led by the same chip and AI stocks that fell hardest, while bond yields and Fed hike odds move higher. Wednesday's GDP and inflation data are the main test of whether the bounce lasts.
